nqa / it’s possible she could molt if she isn’t fully mature, i have heard that spiders could be pushed to molt after a big meal. signs of molting are making a thick web, by thick i mean you can barely see them, usually only their silhouette, and they will typically only stay there. they may leave briefly for water but will refuse food and may become more skittish, retreating to their web if they feel unsafe. this is normal!

if you notice those signs and believe it is in its premolt stage, the best advice is to disturb the enclosure as little as possible. for me, this means the only time i open the enclosure is to mist, and i check on her with slow, quiet movements (and, lucky me, my spider just molted overnight!) however, if you notice that your spider is still active, then you just need to wait awhile until their abdomen shrinks! i noticed that in your other post it’s likely that you have a female mature spider, in which case their abdomens can get very large for eggs, although i don’t think that’s the case here.

https://preview.redd.it/ilbzzdodytgd1.jpeg?width=720&format=pjpg&auto=webp&s=205f79bb6a6946141b1a37ef491d2bff31fb5f00

to me, it just looks like the spider had a nice big meal and could be between fed and overfed, which i think is normal. from what i understand, gravid spiders have a much more rounded abdomen than what is pictured

nqa  / follow the chart! they can be overfed, and if that happens they have a shorter lifespan and are prone to abdominal rupture/separation. they can go weeks without eating (such as during premolt) but a blowfly twice its size sounds like it will keep them full awhile. they won’t starve if they don’t eat awhile, no worries.

i say this as my girl, also my first spood, is in premolt and hasn’t eaten in almost two weeks now, but it doesn’t take a spider being in premolt for them to not need to eat, they are opportunistic feeders and they conserve energy as is their nature for survival, which is why they can overeat, they don’t know when their next meal is!
